title: Jay Wright molded Jalen Brunson and the Nova Knicks. He watched them In their moment of glory, he was watching – on his phone, from his car | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

On Saturday night, Jay Wright was in Red Bank, New Jersey, to attend the wedding of the daughter of his wife’s college roommate, doing what so many others were doing in the Tri-State Area –watching the NBA Finals on his phone.

The former Villanova coach watched the first half of Game 5 inside the reception, but as the fourth quarter played out, he searched for somewhere away from thecrowd to watch the Knicks and the Spurs.

Which is how Wright – the man who first putJalen Brunson, Josh Hart and Mikal Bridgestogether on a team – came to watch his former players capture the NBA championship from the front seat of his car, with no one around him but his wife, Patty.

He couldn’t have drawn it up better if he tried.

As New York wakes up from its two-day weekend bender to a glorious Monday with their Knicks as NBA champions, Wright is only now emerging from his own personal media blockade. He had declined interview requests and deflected attention throughout the playoffs; he even tried to beg out of going to Game 4, reluctantly agreeing to go to the Garden only after Jalen’s dad and Knicks’ assistant Rick Brunson insisted.

Though always a magnet who turned heads like Elvis when he walked into a room, Wright detested being the star of any show. After wins, he deflected praise. After losses, he assumed blame. To hear him tell it, his two national championships and Hall of Fame career are the results of some sort of bystander good fortune, earned on the merits of his players’ talents and not his own ingenuity. The last thing he wanted in this last month was to somehow get credit for the Knicks’ success.

“I didn’t want to be out there, with my face all over the place, when the goal hadn’t been accomplished yet,” Wright toldCNN Sports. “It would have been so inauthentic. This was theirs, not mine.”

The joke, though, is on him. Wright’s very genuine display of humility is even more evidence of how his fingerprints are all over this Knicks team.

In a world hellbent on celebrating individualism – selfies and influencers and likes and followers – New York won as a collective. They subsumed their personal quests for greatness in exchange for something bigger than themselves.

As the playoffs wore on, the Knicks refused to admire their accomplishments and instead kept focusing on the mistakes they made or where they needed to improve. Brunson turned off his social media and Hart at one point even stopped responding to his coach via text, offering only an occasional thumbs up.

“They understood that we’re in this process and we have to learn,” Wright said. “There’s no celebrating the previous game. It’s not going to do any good. It’s that mental toughness, that’s why they won.”

What the coach left unsaid is that all of that is the very essence of what he preached in his career at Villanova. He urged his players to embrace the long-lost concept of the greater good, and to believe that, by accomplishing as a whole, they’d achieve what they wanted personally.

In the corner of the team’s theater room, Wright hung a chart that was updated regularly by the team’s leader in attitude points, awarded for out-of-the-box accomplishments such as diving on the floor for loose balls or taking charges. The concept became so ingrained at Villanova that the word became near Pavlovian.

The Wildcats broke huddles saying, “Attitude.” They high-fived each other and shouted it at each other when attitude was properly displayed, and used it like a dog cuss if it wasn’t.

And it went deeper than words. The one true fallacy of Wright’s coaching success is that everyone presumes he was a nice guy to play for. He was not. He was, in fact, a hard ass, a wolf dressed in bespoke clothing who would not abide a lack of effort and saw selfishness as a personal affront.

The combination – the buzzwords drilled down by a drill sergeant – coalesced into a team that was as mentally tough as it was talented. When Villanova got things rolling, it did not just win games; it broke opponents’ will. In 2016, the Wildcats turned Buddy Hield into a shell of himself in the national semifinal and in 2018, the Cats won their six NCAA Tournament games by an average of 17.6 points per game. No one got within double digits.

Wright insists that whatever leg up all of that gave his players is small compared to the leaps they’ve made on their own.

“There are certain things we taught them but with their own intelligence, experiences and the families around them, they took it to another level,” Wright said. “We didn’t know the pro game. That wasn’t our job. We could only help them so much.”

Yet think about the Knicks, a team in which three-fifths of the starters learned from Wright.

Brunson declined a bigger payout so his franchise could win. Hart willingly did the dirty work, snatching up rebounds rather than points. Bridges took the heat from fans after lackluster performances early on and kept his head down.

Now mix in the rest of the key players:Karl-Anthony Townsleft a team where he was a star to join a team where he’d be among them.Jose Alvaradocame off the bench like a fire starter. Landry Shamet came back in Game 5 after leaving with a leg injury. Mitchell Robinson played essentially with a club on his right hand, not to mention a broken pinky.

And remember what these Knicks did: They started the playoffs down 2-1 to the Atlanta Hawks and proceeded to win 13 games in a row. In 19 postseason games, they won 16 and never once faced an elimination game. In each of their four wins against the Spurs, they trailed by double digits. In Game 3, Towns was the hero. In Game 4, it was OG Anunoby and in 5, it was Brunson.

Then pause and think about Jay Wright. About a Hall of Fame coach with a chance to witness his three players make history, choosing instead to sneak off in a car to watch, all so he wouldn’t disturb a wedding.

He is the Nova in the Knicks.
